raw_tool_response: User responded: provisioning=ACCOUNT PROVISIONING AND TENANT / ROLE ASSIGNMENT POLICY  1. INITIAL PLATFORM ADMIN BOOTSTRAP  - The initial Platform Admin must be created through a secure, controlled, one-time deployment/bootstrap process. - Public registration, ordinary user registration, or self-service signup must never grant Platform Admin privileges. - The bootstrap process must establish the initial Platform Admin identity using a verified identity and secure authentication. - Bootstrap credentials or temporary secrets must not remain active after successful provisioning. - Bootstrap execution and initial privileged account creation must be auditable. - Subsequent Platform Admin assignments must require explicit authorization from an existing authorized Platform Admin and must be independently audited. - Self-promotion to Platform Admin is prohibited.  2. TENANT CREATION AND INITIAL ADMINISTRATION  - Only an authorized Platform Admin may create a new tenant. - The Platform Admin must assign an initial Tenant Admin during tenant provisioning. - Tenant creation, tenant identity, initial administrator assignment, and provisioning events must be recorded in an audit history. - A Tenant Admin must have administrative authority only within their assigned tenant. - Tenant Admins must not create, access, or administer other tenants.  3. USER ACCOUNT PROVISIONING  - An authorized Tenant Admin may invite, provision, activate, deactivate, and manage users within their own tenant, subject to the platform's authentication and identity-verification controls. - Each user must be associated with an explicitly assigned tenant. - User registration or authentication alone must not grant access to tenant resources without an authorized tenant assignment. - A user must not be able to assign themselves to another tenant or elevate their own privileges. - Cross-tenant user assignment and access are prohibited unless explicitly authorized through a separately governed platform-level process.  4. ROLE ASSIGNMENT AND REVOCATION  - The Tenant Admin may grant and revoke standard tenant-scoped roles such as Support Agent and Support Manager within their own tenant. - Knowledge Reviewer must be a separate, explicitly granted permission or role. - Granting Tenant Admin or Support Manager status alone must not automatically grant Knowledge Reviewer authority. - Knowledge Reviewer assignment must be explicitly authorized and recorded with the assigning administrator, tenant, user, permission, and timestamp. - The original document submitter must never approve their own document or revision, regardless of their assigned roles. - Users must not grant, modify, or remove their own privileged permissions. - Role changes and revocations must take effect through enforced authorization controls and be auditable.  5. PRIVILEGED ROLE PROTECTION  - Platform Admin privileges must remain separate from tenant-level administrative permissions. - Platform Admins must not automatically receive routine access to tenant knowledge content or approval authority. - Tenant Admins must not be able to grant Platform Admin privileges. - Privileged role assignments and removals must require explicit authorization and audit logging. - Authentication and authorization must be enforced at the API and data-access layers, not only through the user interface.  6. FIRST-RELEASE EXCEPTIONAL ACCESS POLICY  - No exceptional cross-tenant content access, emergency knowledge approval, or privileged bypass mechanism is permitted in the first demonstrable release. - Platform Admin access is limited to platform-level administration and operational metadata required for platform management. - Platform Admin status must not bypass tenant isolation, Knowledge Reviewer independence, document approval, or audit requirements. - Any future emergency or break-glass access capability must require a separate approved requirement, explicit authorization, a defined purpose, time limitation, and comprehensive audit logging.  7. AUDITABILITY  The system must maintain an auditable record of: - Initial bootstrap and Platform Admin creation. - Tenant creation and initial Tenant Admin assignment. - User invitations, provisioning, activation, and deactivation. - Tenant assignments and role grants/revocations. - Knowledge Reviewer permission assignments and removals. - Privileged administrative actions and authorization failures.  All account and permission operations must follow least-privilege principles, tenant isolation, and the established separation-of-duties requirements.  These decisions define first-release provisioning and privilege boundaries only. They do not authorize implementation, runtime access, or any unapproved privileged operation., account_lifecycle=ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT, REACTIVATION AND RECOVERY POLICY  1. ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT AUTHORITY  - An authorized Platform Admin may disable platform-level accounts and manage platform-level account access. - An authorized Tenant Admin may disable or suspend user accounts belonging exclusively to their own tenant. - Support Managers and other users may report security concerns or request account disablement but cannot independently execute privileged account administration actions unless explicitly authorized. - Tenant Admins must not administer accounts belonging to other tenants. - Users must not disable or modify their own privileged status to bypass established administrative controls. - Disabling the last active Platform Admin or the last authorized Tenant Admin must require an independently authorized administrative recovery process to prevent administrative lockout.  2. IMMEDIATE ACCESS REVOCATION  When an account is disabled or suspended:  - Block new authentication and login attempts. - Immediately revoke all active sessions and refresh tokens. - Invalidate existing access tokens through enforced account-status and authorization checks. - Terminate active application sessions and prevent further API access. - Remove the user's effective access to tenant resources and protected knowledge. - Prevent further privileged operations. - Preserve the account identity, audit history, and relevant business records. - Record the actor, reason, timestamp, affected tenant, and resulting access-revocation events.  Account disablement must take effect across all application entry points, APIs, and relevant data-access operations, not merely through UI restrictions.  3. ACCOUNT REACTIVATION  - Only an authorized administrator responsible for the relevant account and tenant may reactivate a disabled account. - Reactivation requires verified user identity and an explicit administrative decision. - The administrator must review the original disablement reason and confirm that the reason for suspension has been resolved. - Security-compromised accounts must complete the applicable security remediation and identity-verification checks before reactivation. - Reactivation must not automatically restore previously privileged roles. - Standard roles may be reassigned following verification of current employment, tenant membership, and business authorization. - Platform Admin, Tenant Admin, and Knowledge Reviewer permissions require separate explicit authorization. - The original submitter restriction and independent knowledge approval requirements remain unchanged.  4. ACCOUNT RECOVERY  - Password recovery and authentication-factor recovery must use the configured trusted identity provider's secure recovery mechanisms. - Recovery must require appropriate identity verification. - Administrative password sharing, insecure credential resets, and informal MFA bypasses are prohibited. - Recovery must not grant additional roles, tenant membership, or administrative privileges. - Recovery of a compromised account must include appropriate credential rotation and revocation of existing sessions and tokens. - All recovery actions and outcomes must be auditable.  5. SELF-ESCALATION AND RECOVERY BYPASS PREVENTION  - Users must never grant themselves additional roles, permissions, or tenant assignments. - A Tenant Admin must not grant themselves Platform Admin or unauthorized Knowledge Reviewer privileges. - Account recovery must not bypass authentication, MFA, tenant isolation, or role authorization requirements. - An administrator must not use account recovery to circumvent a previous security suspension. - Privileged role restoration requires explicit authorization separate from ordinary account reactivation. - The system must reject unauthorized account-state transitions and privilege changes.  6. ADMINISTRATIVE LOCKOUT AND RECOVERY  - The first release must prevent accidental removal or disablement of the last active authorized Platform Admin or last authorized Tenant Admin without an independently authorized recovery path. - Platform-level administrative recovery must use a controlled and auditable out-of-band process. - No ordinary user or Tenant Admin may independently elevate themselves to recover administrative access. - Recovery must preserve tenant boundaries and existing separation-of-duties restrictions.  7. AUDITABILITY  The system must maintain auditable records of: - Account disablement and suspension. - Reactivation requests and decisions. - Identity verification and recovery events. - Session and token revocation. - Role and tenant assignment changes. - Privileged permission restoration. - Administrative lockout prevention and recovery actions. - Failed and unauthorized access or recovery attempts. This policy preserves the first-release prohibition established in Q4 and does not authorize implementation or runtime access., audit_rationale=PRIVILEGED ACCESS AUDIT, EVIDENCE, RATIONALE AND EXPLICIT DEFERRALS  1. AUDIT EVENTS AND REQUIRED FIELDS  The system must maintain tamper-resistant, access-controlled audit records for all privileged account-management and authorization events.  A. ROLE AND PERMISSION GRANTS Record: - Event ID and timestamp (UTC). - Actor identity and assigned administrative role. - Target user identity and tenant ID. - Granted role or permission. - Previous and resulting permission state. - Authorization or approval reference. - Reason or business justification. - Operation outcome.  B. PRIVILEGED PERMISSION USAGE Record: - Actor identity and tenant context. - Privileged operation performed. - Target account, resource, or permission reference. - Operation timestamp. - Authorization decision. - Success or failure outcome. - Correlation or request ID.  C. ACCESS DENIAL AND UNAUTHORIZED ATTEMPTS Record: - Attempted actor identity, where available. - Requested operation and target resource. - Relevant tenant context. - Denial reason or authorization failure category. - Timestamp and correlation ID. - Security-relevant outcome.  D. ACCOUNT RECOVERY AND REACTIVATION Record: - Account identity and tenant. - Recovery or reactivation event type. - Requesting and authorizing administrator identities, where applicable. - Identity-verification outcome. - Recovery or reactivation reason. - Previous and resulting account status. - Timestamp and operation outcome.  E. SESSION AND TOKEN REVOCATION Record: - Affected user and account. - Revocation event type. - Initiating actor or system process. - Revocation reason. - Event timestamp. - Revocation execution outcome. - Relevant session or token reference identifiers, without recording actual token values.  F. PERMISSION EXPIRY AND REVOCATION Record: - Affected user, tenant, role, and permission. - Expiry or revocation reason. - Initiating actor or authorized system process. - Effective timestamp. - Previous and resulting permission state. - Execution outcome.  2. AUDIT DATA PROTECTION AND SECRET EXCLUSIONS  Audit records must contain sufficient metadata to establish accountability without exposing sensitive credentials or unnecessary business content.  The following must never be recorded in plaintext audit logs: - Passwords or password hashes. - Access tokens or refresh tokens. - API keys, client secrets, or private cryptographic keys. - MFA secrets, one-time passwords, or recovery codes. - Complete authentication credentials. - Unnecessary customer personal information. - Full customer conversations, ticket content, or Knowledge Base documents. - Unnecessary copies of confidential tenant business data.  Use stable identifiers, event references, reason codes, and appropriately redacted metadata instead of storing sensitive source content.  3. AUDIT INTEGRITY AND ACCESS CONTROL  - Audit records must be protected against unauthorized modification and deletion. - Ordinary users and Tenant Admins must not modify or erase historical audit evidence. - Audit access must be restricted to explicitly authorized administrative and security roles. - Tenant-level audit access must respect tenant isolation. - Platform Admins must not gain access to tenant content merely through audit privileges. - Failed, denied, and unauthorized privileged operations must also be recorded. - Audit events must be correlated across account provisioning, authorization, session management, and recovery workflows. - Audit logging failures affecting security-critical operations must be handled safely and must not silently permit unauthorized privilege changes.  4. RATIONALE  This audit framework establishes accountability, traceability, and evidence for privileged operations.  It enables security investigations, verification of administrative decisions, detection of unauthorized privilege escalation, and reconstruction of account and permission changes.  Recording both successful and unsuccessful operations provides visibility into legitimate administrative activity as well as attempted security violations.  Excluding credentials, secrets, and unnecessary customer content reduces the risk that the audit system itself becomes a source of sensitive-data exposure.  The approach supports least privilege, tenant isolation, separation of duties, and the previously established independent knowledge approval requirements.  5. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED DECISIONS  The following operational and technical details are not finalized through this decision:  - Exact audit-log retention and archival periods. - Detailed database schema and audit-event storage implementation. - SIEM integration and centralized security-monitoring architecture. - Alert severity classifications, notification channels, and incident-response SLAs. - Detailed audit-log backup, disaster recovery, and long-term evidence preservation procedures. - Formal compliance certification and jurisdiction-specific retention requirements.  These matters may be addressed through subsequent governed requirement clarification and appropriate security review.  6. CONSISTENCY WITH PREVIOUS Q2, Q3 AND Q4 DECISIONS  All audit and privileged-access controls must preserve the previously established decisions:  - Tenant-scoped RBAC and least-privilege enforcement. - Independent Knowledge Reviewer authorization. - Prohibition of self-approval. - Controlled account provisioning and role assignment. - Immediate session and token revocation following account disablement. - No automatic restoration of privileged permissions during reactivation. - Prohibition of exceptional Platform Admin tenant-content access in the first release. - No unauthorized cross-tenant access or privilege escalation.  This decision establishes the first-release audit and accountability requirements only. It does not constitute Requirement approval, implementation authorization, or permission to access tenant content.

actual_fields.expiry_revocation: EXCEPTION EXPIRY, REVOCATION AND OVERSIGHT POLICY  For the first demonstrable release, exceptional Platform Admin tenant-content access is strictly prohibited, as established in the preceding Q4 decision.  Accordingly:  1. No exceptional tenant-content access grants, temporary access sessions, emergency access tokens, or break-glass permissions may be created or issued.  2. Since no such exceptions are permitted, no exception expiry mechanism, exception-specific revocation owner, or exception oversight workflow is required for the first release.  3. Platform Admins must not bypass this restriction through direct database access, application APIs, administrative tools, support procedures, or alternative authentication mechanisms.  4. Any existing unauthorized or improperly granted tenant-content access must be revoked immediately, including associated active sessions and tokens, and the incident must be recorded and investigated.  5. Normal Platform Admin account disablement, session termination, token revocation, and privileged-account oversight remain governed by the established Q4 account security policies.  6. Any future introduction of exceptional tenant-content access must require separate Requirement Analysis, security and privacy assessment, explicit Human approval, and an independently approved policy defining:    - Authorized approving authority.    - Exact tenant, data, and operation scope.    - Maximum access duration and automatic expiry.    - Revocation triggers and responsible owner.    - Active-session and token termination.    - Audit logging, notifications, and post-access oversight.    - Emergency handling and prohibition of self-authorization.  No exceptional access authority is inferred or granted by this decision.  This policy preserves the first-release prohibition established in Q4 and does not authorize implementation or runtime access.
actual_fields.audit_rationale: PRIVILEGED ACCESS AUDIT, EVIDENCE, RATIONALE AND EXPLICIT DEFERRALS  1. AUDIT EVENTS AND REQUIRED FIELDS  The system must maintain tamper-resistant, access-controlled audit records for all privileged account-management and authorization events.  A. ROLE AND PERMISSION GRANTS Record: - Event ID and timestamp (UTC). - Actor identity and assigned administrative role. - Target user identity and tenant ID. - Granted role or permission. - Previous and resulting permission state. - Authorization or approval reference. - Reason or business justification. - Operation outcome.  B. PRIVILEGED PERMISSION USAGE Record: - Actor identity and tenant context. - Privileged operation performed. - Target account, resource, or permission reference. - Operation timestamp. - Authorization decision. - Success or failure outcome. - Correlation or request ID.  C. ACCESS DENIAL AND UNAUTHORIZED ATTEMPTS Record: - Attempted actor identity, where available. - Requested operation and target resource. - Relevant tenant context. - Denial reason or authorization failure category. - Timestamp and correlation ID. - Security-relevant outcome.  D. ACCOUNT RECOVERY AND REACTIVATION Record: - Account identity and tenant. - Recovery or reactivation event type. - Requesting and authorizing administrator identities, where applicable. - Identity-verification outcome. - Recovery or reactivation reason. - Previous and resulting account status. - Timestamp and operation outcome.  E. SESSION AND TOKEN REVOCATION Record: - Affected user and account. - Revocation event type. - Initiating actor or system process. - Revocation reason. - Event timestamp. - Revocation execution outcome. - Relevant session or token reference identifiers, without recording actual token values.  F. PERMISSION EXPIRY AND REVOCATION Record: - Affected user, tenant, role, and permission. - Expiry or revocation reason. - Initiating actor or authorized system process. - Effective timestamp. - Previous and resulting permission state. - Execution outcome.  2. AUDIT DATA PROTECTION AND SECRET EXCLUSIONS  Audit records must contain sufficient metadata to establish accountability without exposing sensitive credentials or unnecessary business content.  The following must never be recorded in plaintext audit logs: - Passwords or password hashes. - Access tokens or refresh tokens. - API keys, client secrets, or private cryptographic keys. - MFA secrets, one-time passwords, or recovery codes. - Complete authentication credentials. - Unnecessary customer personal information. - Full customer conversations, ticket content, or Knowledge Base documents. - Unnecessary copies of confidential tenant business data.  Use stable identifiers, event references, reason codes, and appropriately redacted metadata instead of storing sensitive source content.  3. AUDIT INTEGRITY AND ACCESS CONTROL  - Audit records must be protected against unauthorized modification and deletion. - Ordinary users and Tenant Admins must not modify or erase historical audit evidence. - Audit access must be restricted to explicitly authorized administrative and security roles. - Tenant-level audit access must respect tenant isolation. - Platform Admins must not gain access to tenant content merely through audit privileges. - Failed, denied, and unauthorized privileged operations must also be recorded. - Audit events must be correlated across account provisioning, authorization, session management, and recovery workflows. - Audit logging failures affecting security-critical operations must be handled safely and must not silently permit unauthorized privilege changes.  4. RATIONALE  This audit framework establishes accountability, traceability, and evidence for privileged operations.  It enables security investigations, verification of administrative decisions, detection of unauthorized privilege escalation, and reconstruction of account and permission changes.  Recording both successful and unsuccessful operations provides visibility into legitimate administrative activity as well as attempted security violations.  Excluding credentials, secrets, and unnecessary customer content reduces the risk that the audit system itself becomes a source of sensitive-data exposure.  The approach supports least privilege, tenant isolation, separation of duties, and the previously established independent knowledge approval requirements.  5. EXPLICITLY DEFERRED DECISIONS  The following operational and technical details are not finalized through this decision:  - Exact audit-log retention and archival periods. - Detailed database schema and audit-event storage implementation. - SIEM integration and centralized security-monitoring architecture. - Alert severity classifications, notification channels, and incident-response SLAs. - Detailed audit-log backup, disaster recovery, and long-term evidence preservation procedures. - Formal compliance certification and jurisdiction-specific retention requirements.  These matters may be addressed through subsequent governed requirement clarification and appropriate security review.  6. CONSISTENCY WITH PREVIOUS Q2, Q3 AND Q4 DECISIONS  All audit and privileged-access controls must preserve the previously established decisions:  - Tenant-scoped RBAC and least-privilege enforcement. - Independent Knowledge Reviewer authorization. - Prohibition of self-approval. - Controlled account provisioning and role assignment. - Immediate session and token revocation following account disablement. - No automatic restoration of privileged permissions during reactivation. - Prohibition of exceptional Platform Admin tenant-content access in the first release. - No unauthorized cross-tenant access or privilege escalation.  This decision establishes the first-release audit and accountability requirements only. It does not constitute Requirement approval, implementation authorization, or permission to access tenant content.

provisioning.exact_rendered_segment: ACCOUNT PROVISIONING AND TENANT / ROLE ASSIGNMENT POLICY  1. INITIAL PLATFORM ADMIN BOOTSTRAP  - The initial Platform Admin must be created through a secure, controlled, one-time deployment/bootstrap process. - Public registration, ordinary user registration, or self-service signup must never grant Platform Admin privileges. - The bootstrap process must establish the initial Platform Admin identity using a verified identity and secure authentication. - Bootstrap credentials or temporary secrets must not remain active after successful provisioning. - Bootstrap execution and initial privileged account creation must be auditable. - Subsequent Platform Admin assignments must require explicit authorization from an existing authorized Platform Admin and must be independently audited. - Self-promotion to Platform Admin is prohibited.  2. TENANT CREATION AND INITIAL ADMINISTRATION  - Only an authorized Platform Admin may create a new tenant. - The Platform Admin must assign an initial Tenant Admin during tenant provisioning. - Tenant creation, tenant identity, initial administrator assignment, and provisioning events must be recorded in an audit history. - A Tenant Admin must have administrative authority only within their assigned tenant. - Tenant Admins must not create, access, or administer other tenants.  3. USER ACCOUNT PROVISIONING  - An authorized Tenant Admin may invite, provision, activate, deactivate, and manage users within their own tenant, subject to the platform's authentication and identity-verification controls. - Each user must be associated with an explicitly assigned tenant. - User registration or authentication alone must not grant access to tenant resources without an authorized tenant assignment. - A user must not be able to assign themselves to another tenant or elevate their own privileges. - Cross-tenant user assignment and access are prohibited unless explicitly authorized through a separately governed platform-level process.  4. ROLE ASSIGNMENT AND REVOCATION  - The Tenant Admin may grant and revoke standard tenant-scoped roles such as Support Agent and Support Manager within their own tenant. - Knowledge Reviewer must be a separate, explicitly granted permission or role. - Granting Tenant Admin or Support Manager status alone must not automatically grant Knowledge Reviewer authority. - Knowledge Reviewer assignment must be explicitly authorized and recorded with the assigning administrator, tenant, user, permission, and timestamp. - The original document submitter must never approve their own document or revision, regardless of their assigned roles. - Users must not grant, modify, or remove their own privileged permissions. - Role changes and revocations must take effect through enforced authorization controls and be auditable.  5. PRIVILEGED ROLE PROTECTION  - Platform Admin privileges must remain separate from tenant-level administrative permissions. - Platform Admins must not automatically receive routine access to tenant knowledge content or approval authority. - Tenant Admins must not be able to grant Platform Admin privileges. - Privileged role assignments and removals must require explicit authorization and audit logging. - Authentication and authorization must be enforced at the API and data-access layers, not only through the user interface.  6. FIRST-RELEASE EXCEPTIONAL ACCESS POLICY  - No exceptional cross-tenant content access, emergency knowledge approval, or privileged bypass mechanism is permitted in the first demonstrable release. - Platform Admin access is limited to platform-level administration and operational metadata required for platform management. - Platform Admin status must not bypass tenant isolation, Knowledge Reviewer independence, document approval, or audit requirements. - Any future emergency or break-glass access capability must require a separate approved requirement, explicit authorization, a defined purpose, time limitation, and comprehensive audit logging.  7. AUDITABILITY  The system must maintain an auditable record of: - Initial bootstrap and Platform Admin creation. - Tenant creation and initial Tenant Admin assignment. - User invitations, provisioning, activation, and deactivation. - Tenant assignments and role grants/revocations. - Knowledge Reviewer permission assignments and removals. - Privileged administrative actions and authorization failures.  All account and permission operations must follow least-privilege principles, tenant isolation, and the established separation-of-duties requirements.  These decisions define first-release provisioning and privilege boundaries only. They do not authorize implementation, runtime access, or any unapproved privileged operation.,

account_lifecycle.exact_rendered_segment: ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT, REACTIVATION AND RECOVERY POLICY  1. ACCOUNT DISABLEMENT AUTHORITY  - An authorized Platform Admin may disable platform-level accounts and manage platform-level account access. - An authorized Tenant Admin may disable or suspend user accounts belonging exclusively to their own tenant. - Support Managers and other users may report security concerns or request account disablement but cannot independently execute privileged account administration actions unless explicitly authorized. - Tenant Admins must not administer accounts belonging to other tenants. - Users must not disable or modify their own privileged status to bypass established administrative controls. - Disabling the last active Platform Admin or the last authorized Tenant Admin must require an independently authorized administrative recovery process to prevent administrative lockout.  2. IMMEDIATE ACCESS REVOCATION  When an account is disabled or suspended:  - Block new authentication and login attempts. - Immediately revoke all active sessions and refresh tokens. - Invalidate existing access tokens through enforced account-status and authorization checks. - Terminate active application sessions and prevent further API access. - Remove the user's effective access to tenant resources and protected knowledge. - Prevent further privileged operations. - Preserve the account identity, audit history, and relevant business records. - Record the actor, reason, timestamp, affected tenant, and resulting access-revocation events.  Account disablement must take effect across all application entry points, APIs, and relevant data-access operations, not merely through UI restrictions.  3. ACCOUNT REACTIVATION  - Only an authorized administrator responsible for the relevant account and tenant may reactivate a disabled account. - Reactivation requires verified user identity and an explicit administrative decision. - The administrator must review the original disablement reason and confirm that the reason for suspension has been resolved. - Security-compromised accounts must complete the applicable security remediation and identity-verification checks before reactivation. - Reactivation must not automatically restore previously privileged roles. - Standard roles may be reassigned following verification of current employment, tenant membership, and business authorization. - Platform Admin, Tenant Admin, and Knowledge Reviewer permissions require separate explicit authorization. - The original submitter restriction and independent knowledge approval requirements remain unchanged.  4. ACCOUNT RECOVERY  - Password recovery and authentication-factor recovery must use the configured trusted identity provider's secure recovery mechanisms. - Recovery must require appropriate identity verification. - Administrative password sharing, insecure credential resets, and informal MFA bypasses are prohibited. - Recovery must not grant additional roles, tenant membership, or administrative privileges. - Recovery of a compromised account must include appropriate credential rotation and revocation of existing sessions and tokens. - All recovery actions and outcomes must be auditable.  5. SELF-ESCALATION AND RECOVERY BYPASS PREVENTION  - Users must never grant themselves additional roles, permissions, or tenant assignments. - A Tenant Admin must not grant themselves Platform Admin or unauthorized Knowledge Reviewer privileges. - Account recovery must not bypass authentication, MFA, tenant isolation, or role authorization requirements. - An administrator must not use account recovery to circumvent a previous security suspension. - Privileged role restoration requires explicit authorization separate from ordinary account reactivation. - The system must reject unauthorized account-state transitions and privilege changes.  6. ADMINISTRATIVE LOCKOUT AND RECOVERY  - The first release must prevent accidental removal or disablement of the last active authorized Platform Admin or last authorized Tenant Admin without an independently authorized recovery path. - Platform-level administrative recovery must use a controlled and auditable out-of-band process. - No ordinary user or Tenant Admin may independently elevate themselves to recover administrative access. - Recovery must preserve tenant boundaries and existing separation-of-duties restrictions.  7. AUDITABILITY  The system must maintain auditable records of: - Account disablement and suspension. - Reactivation requests and decisions. - Identity verification and recovery events. - Session and token revocation. - Role and tenant assignment changes. - Privileged permission restoration. - Administrative lockout prevention and recovery actions. - Failed and unauthorized access or recovery attempts.  All operations must be tenant-scoped where applicable, enforce least privilege, and comply with the established Q2 and Q3 governance decisions.  These policies define first-release account security boundaries and do not authorize implementation or runtime access.,

role_permissions.exact_rendered_segment: ACCOUNT-MANAGEMENT ROLE PERMISSION MATRIX  Apply least-privilege, tenant-scoped RBAC. Account-management permissions must remain separate from knowledge review and approval permissions.  1. PLATFORM ADMIN  - Create, configure, suspend, and manage tenants at the platform level. - Assign the initial Tenant Admin during tenant provisioning. - Manage platform-level accounts and authorized Platform Admin assignments. - Perform platform-level account disablement and reactivation. - Manage platform operational configuration and account administration. - Must not automatically receive Knowledge Reviewer authority or routine access to tenant knowledge content. - Must not bypass tenant isolation, independent approval, or self-approval restrictions.  2. TENANT ADMIN  - Invite, provision, activate, deactivate, suspend, and reactivate users within their own tenant. - Assign and revoke standard tenant roles, including Support Agent and Support Manager. - Explicitly assign and revoke Knowledge Reviewer permissions within their own tenant. - Request and manage account recovery through the authorized identity and recovery process. - Manage tenant-level user membership and access. - Must not create tenants, assign Platform Admin privileges, or administer other tenants. - Tenant Admin status alone must not grant Knowledge Reviewer authority.  3. SUPPORT MANAGER  - View and manage authorized support-team operational information within their tenant. - Report account-security concerns and request user disablement or access changes from the Tenant Admin. - Monitor relevant support-team access and operational activities where authorized. - Must not independently create users, assign roles, reactivate accounts, or grant privileged permissions. - Knowledge approval is permitted only if separately assigned the Knowledge Reviewer permission and the non-submitter rule is satisfied.  4. SUPPORT AGENT  - Access support functions and customer/ticket information permitted by their tenant-scoped role. - Use approved and currently eligible Knowledge Base content. - Report suspected security issues or request account assistance. - Use authorized self-service authentication and account-recovery mechanisms. - Must not create or manage other user accounts, assign roles, change tenant membership, or grant permissions. - Must not approve, reject, expire, delete, or reinstate knowledge unless separately authorized through an explicitly permitted role, subject to all independent-review restrictions.  5. KNOWLEDGE REVIEWER  - Review submitted knowledge documents within explicitly assigned tenants. - Approve or reject documents and revisions submitted by other users. - Resolve assigned knowledge reliability flags and authorize reinstatement when applicable. - Perform authorized knowledge expiry and review decisions under the established lifecycle policy. - Must not automatically receive account-management, user-provisioning, or tenant-administration permissions. - May hold another administrative role only through a separate explicit role assignment. - Must never approve their own submission or revision.  6. CROSS-ROLE AND SECURITY RESTRICTIONS  - Administrative permissions and Knowledge Reviewer permissions must be independently assigned and enforced. - No role automatically grants additional privileges merely because it is considered senior or administrative. - Users must not assign privileges to themselves or elevate their own access. - Tenant Admins may administer only users and resources belonging to their own tenant. - Platform Admins must not have routine tenant knowledge-content access or automatic knowledge approval authority. - Account disablement must revoke sessions, tokens, and effective access as established in Q4. - Reactivation must not automatically restore privileged roles. - The last active Platform Admin or Tenant Admin must be protected against accidental lockout. - All account creation, role assignment, permission changes, disablement, reactivation, and recovery actions must be auditable. - Authorization must be enforced at API and data-access levels, not merely through UI restrictions.  7. PRESERVATION OF EXISTING KNOWLEDGE GOVERNANCE  The previously established Q2 and Q3 restrictions remain unchanged:  - Document submitters cannot approve their own submissions or revisions. - Tenant Admin or Support Manager status alone does not grant Knowledge Reviewer authority. - An explicitly assigned, eligible non-submitter reviewer is required for knowledge approval and reinstatement. - AI-generated flags cannot grant permissions or independently alter knowledge lifecycle states. - Tenant isolation, current validity, approval status, and the mandatory 180-day re-review policy must always be enforced.  These permissions define the first-release account-management boundaries and do not authorize implementation or runtime access.,
